extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in crowd psychology, mass persuasion, rhetoric, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria about how crowds think, feel, and are influenced; useful for composing messages, speeches, or public appeals aimed at mass audiences. Focuses on what images, arguments, and forms of presentation succeed or fail with crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and exaggeration of crowd sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the feelings exhibited by a crowd are very simple and very exaggerated; individuals in crowds are inaccessible to fine distinctions and see things as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd emotions are heightened by suggestion and contagion; a crowd is blind to intermediate phases and goes at once to extremes (e.g., a suspicion becomes incontrovertible evidence). This lowers nuance and favors broad, amplified appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds are only impressed by excessive sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A crowd is only impressed by excessive, amplified emotions or claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An orator wishing to move a crowd must 'make an abusive use of violent affirmations. To exaggerate, to affirm, to resort to repetitions, and never to attempt to prove anything by reasoning' — methods well known to speakers at public meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to amplify heroes and protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: A crowd demands amplified, exaggerated virtues in its heroes; apparent qualities must be magnified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On stage and in public life, crowds expect heroes to exhibit degrees of courage and virtue not found in real life; political and cultural leaders are therefore often presented in mythic terms to satisfy mass expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of doubt and critical spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds know neither doubt nor uncertainty; they accept or reject ideas wholesale and lack a critical spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because crowds are influenced by suggestion rather than reasoning, contradictory ideas may coexist and the crowd will not perceive logical contradictions; judgments are 'forced upon them' rather than adopted after discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of individual responsibility and impunity effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of responsibility within crowds and the 'certainty of impunity' increases the force and extremity of their sentiments and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The larger the crowd, the stronger the sense of impunity, enabling acts impossible for isolated individuals and freeing foolish or envious persons from awareness of insignificance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas must be absolute, uncompromising, and simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas can influence crowds only after assuming a very absolute, uncompromising, and simple shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lofty philosophic or scientific ideas must be transformed and simplified—often belittled—to become accessible to crowds; social influence depends on form, not intrinsic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds think in images; imagery over abstract argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are primarily impressed by images; they think and are motivated in figurative, imagistic terms rather than abstract reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The marvellous and legendary are the 'real pillars of civilisation' for crowds. Theatrical representations and clear visual or narrative images produce shared emotions and potent influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present condensed, startling images; avoid genesis/explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective presentations to crowds must offer a startling, very clear image, freed from accessory explanation; the genesis of the fact should not be indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hundred petty events won't strike the imagination, whereas a single great, visible event will. Things must be laid before the crowd 'as a whole.' Avoid step-by-step logical exposition; emphasize the single striking scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marvellous and spectacular outrank statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds respond far more to spectacular, marvellous events than to statistical facts or dispersed tragedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an epidemic causing thousands of deaths (presented as statistics) makes less impression than a single dramatic public accident; the probable loss of an Atlantic liner captured the public imagination despite many more ordinary shipwrecks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning and chains of logical argument are ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are not to be influenced by formal reasoning; chains of logical argumentation are incomprehensible to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasion should not rely on demonstration or sophisticated rationale; instead, evoke images and associations that resonate emotionally and unconsciously with the crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferior associative reasoning (apparent analogies and generalisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'reasoning' of crowds is associative and of an inferior order: they associate dissimilar things by apparent connections and immediately generalise particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields fallacious inferences (e.g., extrapolating from one employer's bad behaviour to all employers). Persuaders exploit such associative links rather than formal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence requires penetration into the unconscious/sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea must enter the domain of the unconscious—become a sentiment—to exert irresistible influence on crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implantation of powerful ideas takes long time and eradication is equally slow (e.g., philosophical ideas behind the French Revolution took nearly a century to implant). Superficial acceptance is not enough to change mass behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds are suggestionable and often cannot distinguish the unreal from the real
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are highly suggestionable; the unreal (theatrical or imagined) has nearly as much influence as the real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reflection is suspended, images evoke intense impressions; spectators sometimes react to imaginary crimes as if real, and suggestion can produce action when strong enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds are intolerant and despotic in attitude toward dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds accept or reject beliefs absolutely and are disposed to give authoritative effect to their inspirations; they are intolerant of contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At public meetings, the slightest contradiction may be met with howls, invective, blows, or expulsion; crowds show a docile respect for force and little respect for kindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward conservatism despite episodic violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although crowds may display violent or revolutionary outbursts, they are fundamentally conservative and quickly return to order and servitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds' hereditary and unconscious influences make them resistant to deep institutional change; revolutions often change superficial forms rather than essential structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds can display loftiest virtues (self-sacrifice, devotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are capable of very high moral displays—abnegation, self-sacrifice, disinterested devotion—often exceeding isolated individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals to glory, honour, and patriotism can elicit sacrifices (e.g., Crusaders, volunteers of 1793); collectivities can act disinterestedly and unconsciously for ideals they scarcely understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre and spectacle are powerful levers of mass feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical representations and spectacles produce synchronized emotions in crowds and therefore have enormous influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the audience experiences the same emotions simultaneously, theatre can provoke strong reactions—examples include audiences ready to attack an actor playing a traitor or wildly enthusing over plays that were previously rejected by managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictory ideas can coexist in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds (and certain individuals) often hold simultaneously contradictory ideas because the ideas function as isolated images without logical connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is illustrated in individuals exposed to competing cultural inheritances (e.g., Western-educated Hindoos showing contradictory sets of acts or utterances), and explains how the same crowd can perform dissimilar acts under different stimuli.
